q: Why can solid copper conduct electricity while solid copper iodide cannot?
o: Copper contains mobile delocalised electrons, while CuI has ions fixed within its lattice.
Copper contains mobile positive ions, while CuI contains electrons trapped between its ions.
Copper has weak metallic bonds, while CuI has strong covalent bonds preventing charge movement.
Copper contains free protons, while CuI has neutral particles arranged throughout its lattice.

q: A student strikes samples of copper and copper iodide with a hammer. Why are their behaviours different?
o: CuI contains molecular layers that separate, while copper contains fixed positive and negative ions.
Copper has directional covalent bonds, while CuI has metallic bonds that resist changes in shape.
Copper's bonding can remain attractive as layers shift, while displaced CuI ions can experience repulsion.
CuI has mobile electrons that weaken its lattice, while copper contains neutral atoms that remain bonded.

q: Which combination correctly identifies the particles and attractive forces in solid iodine, I₂?
o: Iodide ions held together by strong electrostatic attractions
I₂ molecules held together by weak intermolecular attractions
Iodine atoms connected throughout a continuous covalent network
I₂ molecules held together by strong ionic attractions

q: Which observation provides the strongest evidence that an unknown solid could be ionic?
o: It conducts electricity as a solid and remains conductive when dissolved.
It is brittle and conducts electricity after its ions become mobile in solution.
It is malleable because charged particles can move through its lattice structure.
It has a low melting point because its covalent bonds require little energy to break.

q: Why can an ionic substance conduct electricity when dissolved in water?
o: Water converts the ions into delocalised electrons that carry electrical charge.
Dissolving breaks the ions into neutral atoms that transfer electrons between molecules.
Water removes the charges from the ions, allowing them to move through the solution.
The ions become mobile in solution and can therefore transport electrical charge.

q: Silicon dioxide, SiO₂, has a very high melting point. Which explanation best accounts for this?
o: Many strong covalent bonds throughout its network require substantial energy to overcome.
Individual SiO₂ molecules have strong intermolecular attractions that require substantial energy to overcome.
Silicon ions and oxide ions form a lattice containing freely moving delocalised electrons.
Weak intermolecular attractions act throughout the structure but occur in very large numbers.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an intramolecular force from an intermolecular force in water?
o: Intramolecular forces attract separate H₂O molecules, while intermolecular forces join H to O.
Intramolecular forces are covalent bonds within H₂O, while intermolecular forces act between molecules.
Intramolecular forces involve lone pairs only, while intermolecular forces involve bonding pairs only.
Intramolecular forces are temporary attractions, while intermolecular forces are permanent covalent bonds.

q: Why does methane have a tetrahedral arrangement around its central carbon?
o: Four regions of electron density repel and arrange themselves for maximum separation.
Four hydrogen nuclei attract one another and arrange themselves at maximum separation.
Carbon's four lone pairs repel one another and force the hydrogen atoms outward.
Four carbon-hydrogen bonds attract one another and form the most compact arrangement.

q: What is the main structural difference between CH₄ and NH₃ described in the exam?
o: CH₄ has three bonding regions and one lone pair, while NH₃ has four bonding regions.
CH₄ has four bonding regions, while NH₃ has three bonding regions and one lone pair.
CH₄ contains four electron regions, while NH₃ contains only three electron regions in total.
CH₄ contains a double bond, while NH₃ contains only single covalent bonds and lone electrons.

q: A central atom has four regions of electron density: three bonding regions and one lone pair. Which shape best matches the exam's model?
o: Linear because the bonding electrons arrange themselves opposite one another
Tetrahedral because all four regions contain atoms attached to the centre
Trigonal pyramidal because one of the four electron regions is non-bonding
Trigonal planar because only three regions contain covalently bonded atoms

q: Which substance meets the definition of a hydrocarbon used in the exam?
o: CH₃OH, because its main structure contains carbon and hydrogen atoms
C₂H₄, because the compound contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms
CO₂, because carbon is covalently bonded to another non-metal element
CH₃COOH, because carbon and hydrogen form the molecule's main backbone

q: Why is fractional distillation effective for separating crude oil?
o: Hydrocarbons have different boiling points associated with differences in their molecular structures.
Hydrocarbons have different electrical charges that cause them to migrate through the fractionating column.
Hydrocarbons react with the column at different temperatures to produce separate chemical products.
Hydrocarbons have different solubilities, causing longer molecules to dissolve near the column's base.

q: Where would the more volatile fractions generally be collected in a fractionating column?
o: Nearer the bottom because volatile hydrocarbons require higher temperatures before condensing
Nearer the top because volatile hydrocarbons remain gaseous until reaching lower temperatures
Nearer the middle because all volatile compounds condense at approximately the same temperature
Nearer the bottom because short-chain molecules have stronger intermolecular attractions

q: Which structural feature identifies propyne rather than propane or propene?
o: A carbon-carbon single bond within a saturated carbon backbone
A carbon-carbon double bond within an unsaturated carbon backbone
A carbon-carbon triple bond within an unsaturated carbon backbone
A carbon-hydrogen triple bond attached to a saturated carbon backbone

q: Why is propane classified as saturated?
o: Every carbon atom has formed the maximum number of hydrogen attachments possible for that structure.
The carbon chain contains enough hydrogen atoms to form a carbon-carbon double bond.
Every carbon atom contains four hydrogen atoms surrounding its outer electron shell.
The molecule contains equal numbers of carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen covalent bonds.

q: Propene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of platinum to produce propane. What happens during this reaction?
o: Hydrogen replaces a carbon atom and the carbon-carbon double bond remains unchanged.
Hydrogen is added across the double bond, producing a more saturated hydrocarbon.
Hydrogen removes carbon atoms from the chain, producing a shorter saturated hydrocarbon.
Hydrogen causes the molecule to eliminate hydrogen atoms and form a triple bond.

q: Which reaction type best describes the conversion of propene to propane using H₂?
o: Substitution, because hydrogen atoms replace carbon atoms in the original hydrocarbon
Elimination, because hydrogen atoms are removed while a new carbon bond forms
Addition, because atoms are added across the carbon-carbon multiple bond
Combustion, because hydrogen reacts with the hydrocarbon and releases chemical energy

q: When propene reacts with water under acidic conditions, which product is identified as the major product in the exam?
o: Propan-1-ol, because OH preferentially attaches to the more saturated carbon
Propan-2-ol, because OH preferentially attaches to the less saturated carbon
Propane, because hydrogen and hydroxide completely remove the double bond
Propanoic acid, because water oxidises the carbon-carbon double bond

q: Why does ethene produce only one alcohol structure when water is added across its double bond?
o: Both carbon atoms have equivalent environments, so either orientation produces the same product.
One carbon is more saturated, but the hydroxyl group cannot attach to that carbon.
Ethene contains a triple bond, so only one hydrogen atom can enter the structure.
Both carbon atoms contain different numbers of hydrogens but identical numbers of electrons.

q: Which products provide the clearest evidence that a hydrocarbon has undergone complete combustion?
o: Carbon monoxide and water because sufficient oxygen was available
Carbon dioxide and water because sufficient oxygen was available
Carbon dioxide and carbon because oxygen availability was restricted
Carbon monoxide and carbon because excess oxygen was available

q: Which set of products is most consistent with incomplete combustion as represented in the exam?
o: Carbon dioxide and water only
Carbon monoxide, carbon and water
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas
Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen gas

q: Why can a combustion reaction appear to lose mass when performed in an open container?
o: Some atoms are converted directly into thermal energy and leave the reaction mixture.
Carbon atoms are destroyed when chemical bonds release sufficient energy during combustion.
Gaseous products can escape into the surroundings and are no longer included when mass is measured.
Oxygen atoms lose their mass when they form covalent bonds with carbon and hydrogen.

q: Which statement best represents conservation of mass during a chemical reaction?
o: The total number of molecules must remain unchanged throughout every chemical reaction.
The atoms are rearranged into new substances while the number of each type remains constant.
The chemical bonds remain unchanged even though the physical arrangement of particles changes.
The number of products must equal the number of reactants for mass to remain constant.

q: For the equation CH₃CH₂OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O, which atom count is correct on each side?
o: 2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and 7 oxygen atoms
2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms
2 carbon, 5 hydrogen and 7 oxygen atoms
3 carbon, 6 hydrogen and 7 oxygen atoms

q: Which equation represents a decomposition reaction?
o: 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂
CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃
2CO₂ → 2CO + O₂
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

q: What makes 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ a combination reaction?
o: Multiple reactant substances combine to produce a single type of product.
A single reactant substance separates into multiple chemically different products.
An acid reacts with a base to produce an ionic compound and liquid water.
Two ionic solutions exchange ions and produce an insoluble solid product.

q: Carbonic acid is described as diprotic in the exam. What does this indicate?
o: Each carbonic acid species can produce two hydrogen ions during dissociation.
Each carbonic acid species contains two carbonate ions capable of accepting electrons.
Carbonic acid has two carbon atoms capable of forming covalent bonds with hydrogen.
Carbonic acid requires two water molecules before it can behave as an acid.

q: Why does increasing H⁺ concentration lower the pH of seawater?
o: Greater hydrogen-ion concentration corresponds to more acidic conditions.
Greater hydrogen-ion concentration corresponds to more alkaline conditions.
Hydrogen ions react with water to remove all dissolved acidic substances.
Hydrogen ions increase carbonate concentration and therefore raise the solution's pH.

q: HCl reacts with NaOH to produce NaCl and H₂O. Which classification is most appropriate?
o: Precipitation because an insoluble ionic compound forms from two soluble substances
Neutralisation because an acid and base react to produce a salt and water
Decomposition because hydrochloric acid separates into sodium chloride and water
Addition because hydroxide ions are added directly onto hydrochloric acid molecules

q: Which observation would indicate that a neutral solution had been produced after the HCl/NaOH reaction described in the exam?
o: Blue litmus becomes red while red litmus remains unchanged.
Red litmus becomes blue while blue litmus remains unchanged.
Red litmus stays red and blue litmus stays blue.
Both red and blue litmus papers become colourless.

q: What observation is expected when blue cobalt chloride paper detects water?
o: The blue paper becomes pink when exposed to the water product.
The blue paper becomes white when exposed to dissolved chloride ions.
The blue paper becomes red when exposed to a neutral salt solution.
The blue paper remains blue because water does not react with the indicator.

q: What provides the strongest evidence that Reaction Two is a precipitation reaction?
o: Two aqueous ionic substances react and an insoluble solid appears among the products.
An acidic substance reacts with hydroxide ions and produces liquid water molecules.
A covalent substance decomposes and produces two chemically simpler substances.
Two molecular substances combine and produce a single soluble ionic compound.

q: According to collision theory, which collision is most likely to result in a reaction?
o: Particles collide with sufficient energy and an appropriate orientation.
Particles collide at low energy but remain touching for sufficient time.
Particles collide with high frequency regardless of their energy or orientation.
Particles collide at any orientation provided their concentration remains constant.

q: Why does increasing the concentration of a reactant generally increase reaction rate?
o: More reactant particles occupy a given volume, increasing collision frequency.
Each reactant particle becomes larger, increasing the force of every collision.
The activation energy increases, allowing a greater proportion of collisions to succeed.
Reactant particles gain additional electrons, increasing the strength of intermolecular bonding.

q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
o: It increases reactant concentration so that particles collide more frequently.
It provides a pathway requiring less activation energy for successful reaction.
It increases product energy so that the forward reaction becomes more favourable.
It permanently increases particle speed without changing the reaction temperature.

q: Equal concentrations of HCl and CH₃COOH react separately with sodium carbonate. Why does HCl react faster in the exam's comparison?
o: HCl fully dissociates, producing a greater concentration of available hydrogen ions.
CH₃COOH fully dissociates, causing its hydrogen ions to collide less frequently.
HCl contains stronger covalent bonds, so its molecules collide with greater kinetic energy.
CH₃COOH produces more hydrogen ions, but these have insufficient energy for successful collisions.

q: Why can graphite conduct electricity while diamond cannot?
o: Graphite contains delocalised electrons able to carry charge, while diamond lacks mobile charged particles.
Graphite contains mobile carbon ions, while diamond contains carbon atoms fixed by ionic attractions.
Graphite has no covalent bonds between carbon atoms, allowing electrons to move between its layers.
Graphite contains free protons between its layers, while diamond traps its protons inside covalent bonds.

q: Why is graphite soft compared with diamond?
o: Graphite's layers can move over one another because relatively weak attractions act between them.
Graphite contains weak covalent bonds within each layer that readily break when force is applied.
Diamond contains mobile electrons that strengthen its lattice whenever an external force is applied.
Diamond consists of ionic carbon particles arranged in a rigid three-dimensional lattice.

q: Which statement best compares the structures of graphite and diamond?
o: Both are molecular solids, but graphite contains hexagonal molecules while diamond contains tetrahedral molecules.
Both are covalent networks; graphite forms layered structures while diamond forms a three-dimensional network.
Both are ionic lattices; graphite contains mobile ions while diamond contains ions fixed in position.
Both are metallic solids; graphite has delocalised electrons while diamond has localised metal electrons.

q: Which statement best describes the formation of PTFE from tetrafluoroethene?
o: Tetrafluoroethene monomers join as their C=C bonds allow formation of a repeating carbon backbone.
Tetrafluoroethene molecules release fluorine atoms before forming repeating units connected by ionic bonds.
Tetrafluoroethene monomers eliminate water molecules before forming a polymer containing carbon double bonds.
Tetrafluoroethene molecules decompose into carbon fragments that recombine into a covalent network.
